title: DOT vs. non-DOT drug testing: what employers should know
excerpt: Understand the practical differences between federally regulated workplace drug testing and employer-directed screening programs.
content:
Not every workplace drug test follows the same rules. Some employees work in safety-sensitive transportation positions regulated by federal agencies. Others are tested under an employer’s own written policy or applicable state requirements. Knowing which program applies is the first step toward ordering the right service.

What makes a test DOT-regulated?

A Department of Transportation (DOT) test must be conducted under the applicable federal regulations and agency-specific requirements. That can affect the collection procedure, required forms, laboratory process, medical review, and recordkeeping.

For example, covered motor-carrier employers should determine whether their workers fall under Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration requirements rather than assuming every driver is automatically subject to the same program.

  • Determine whether the employee and position are covered by a DOT agency.
  • Identify the required test reason, such as pre-employment or random selection.
  • Use the correct DOT collection workflow and paperwork.

How non-DOT testing differs

A non-DOT test is typically established by the employer’s policy or another applicable rule. Employers may have choices about panels, specimen types, timing, and testing methods, but they still need to consider federal, state, and local law. A non-DOT test does not replace a required DOT test.

Why the distinction matters

Ordering the wrong test type can create compliance problems and delays. Before purchasing, confirm the employee’s role, the reason for testing, the applicable program, and whether a regulated collection process is necessary. If requirements are unclear, consult the program administrator or qualified legal counsel.

Next steps

For regulated transportation programs, review our DOT testing services and compliance resources. For other workplace programs, explore the available testing options and request guidance before a time-sensitive collection.

Related resources: DOT services · Workplace testing

title: Urine, hair, and oral fluid tests: how to choose
excerpt: A clear comparison of common specimen types and the questions to ask before purchasing a screening.
content:
Urine, hair, and oral fluid collections use different specimen types and can serve different screening needs. Choosing between them should begin with the purpose of the test, the applicable program rules, and the services offered at the collection location.

Urine testing

Urine is widely used in workplace testing and is part of many established laboratory workflows. Depending on the program, collections may require specific documentation, identification, and chain-of-custody procedures. The available test panel and procedure should be confirmed before ordering.

Hair testing

Hair testing uses a collected hair specimen and is often selected by programs seeking a different historical view of substance exposure. Hair tests are not interchangeable with every regulated testing program. Collection requirements and interpretations vary by provider and test.

Oral fluid testing

Oral fluid collections use a mouth swab or similar device. They may offer a convenient collection process for certain purposes, but available options depend on the testing panel, laboratory, and regulatory requirements. Ask whether your desired collection method is supported at your chosen site.

Four questions to ask

There is no single best specimen type for every person or employer. Consider:

  • Is the test DOT-regulated or non-DOT?
  • What substances and test panel are required?
  • Which specimen types and collection sites are available?
  • What identification, authorization, and reporting steps apply?

Before scheduling

Read the individual test description and confirm the collection requirements. If the testing program has a written policy, use that policy rather than selecting a method based only on convenience or price.

Related resources: Explore testing options · Get ordering help

title: How to prepare for a drug-testing appointment
excerpt: What to check before heading to a collection site, from identification to donor passes and appointment details.
content:
A successful collection visit usually starts before you reach the testing center. Review your order details and follow the instructions provided for your specific service rather than relying on general advice.

Confirm the order and collection location

Verify the test you purchased, the collection-site address, and whether the site requires an appointment. Some orders require you to select or confirm a location before a donor pass becomes available. If your employer arranged testing, check the instructions they provided.

Bring the right documents

Collection sites commonly verify identity and testing authorization. Bring government-issued identification if instructed, along with the donor pass, registration confirmation, or other paperwork provided for the order. A screenshot or expired authorization may not be accepted at every site.

Follow collection instructions

Read any advance instructions carefully. Requirements may differ by test method and program. Do not attempt to change your specimen or follow online “detox” advice. If you have a medical question, ask the testing provider or an appropriate healthcare professional.

What happens after collection

Once the specimen is collected, processing and review depend on the specific test and service. A completion receipt is not necessarily a final laboratory result. Check the secure customer portal or the communication method designated for your order.

If plans change

If the collection site is closed, your order is missing an authorization, or you cannot attend, contact support before purchasing a second test. Provide your order reference through the approved support channel, but do not send sensitive medical information by ordinary email.

Related resources: Donor passes · Help Center

title: A workplace post-accident testing checklist
excerpt: Practical steps for employers coordinating a collection following a workplace incident.
content:
When a workplace incident occurs, the first priorities are people’s safety, emergency response, and required incident procedures. If your testing policy or a regulation calls for post-accident testing, clear coordination can help avoid unnecessary delays.

Start with safety and policy

Ensure injured people receive appropriate care and follow established emergency procedures. Next, check the employer’s written policy and any DOT or other program rules to understand when a post-accident test is required. Do not assume every incident triggers a regulated test.

Prepare the details the coordinator will need

Having accurate information ready helps a collection provider assess options and availability.

  • An on-site contact person and a reliable callback number.
  • The incident location and the employee’s current location.
  • The required testing type and program (DOT or non-DOT).
  • Whether a clinic visit or a mobile collection is being requested.
  • Relevant authorization and documentation required by the program.

Do not confuse urgency with guaranteed availability

Mobile collection and after-hours support depend on coverage, staffing, and the location. Ask what can actually be arranged and document the steps taken if service is unavailable. Applicable time windows and documentation requirements depend on the governing program.

Protect privacy throughout the process

Share only the information needed to coordinate the collection. Sensitive medical and testing details should travel through authorized secure channels, not informal email or group messages.

Plan before incidents happen

Employers benefit from clear written contact procedures, after-hours escalation paths, and a known process for identifying DOT vs. non-DOT collections. Review these arrangements periodically.

Related resources: Post-accident support · Mobile collections

title: Understanding donor passes and collection authorizations
excerpt: Learn what a donor pass is, when it becomes available, and where to find help before visiting a collection site.
content:
A donor pass or collection authorization connects an order with the person who will provide a specimen. It may include instructions, collection details, and information the testing location needs to process the visit.

When will I receive a donor pass?

Availability depends on the order and the registration steps required for the selected test. A successful payment alone does not always mean that every collection detail is complete. Some services require an assigned collection location before a pass is issued.

Where should I look?

Start with the secure customer portal associated with your order. Review your order information, any issued pass, and instructions that were sent through the approved channel. If you cannot find it, check whether your registration or site selection is still pending.

What should I check before a collection?

Confirm that the donor name, test type, location, and any appointment instructions are correct. Do not use another person’s donor pass or attempt to change information on the pass. Contact support if details appear wrong.

What if the collection site cannot find the order?

If the site cannot accept the authorization, ask for the reason and contact support using your order reference. Keep your purchase information handy. Avoid placing a duplicate order until the status of the original is clarified.

Protect your information

Donor passes and testing results can contain private information. Use the secure customer portal rather than posting documents publicly or sending medical information over ordinary email.

Related resources: Donor pass page · Customer portal

title: Planning a workplace drug and alcohol testing program
excerpt: Build a clearer testing process by defining policy, people, collection methods, and secure result handling.
content:
A workplace testing program involves more than selecting a laboratory panel. Employers need policies, responsible people, ordering procedures, and a practical way to handle collections, results, and follow-up.

Define the reason for testing

Begin with the workforce and applicable legal requirements. Identify whether any employees are subject to DOT rules, which roles are covered by a non-DOT policy, and which testing events may occur. A regulated program should not be replaced with an ordinary non-DOT order.

Put the policy in writing

A written policy can help employees and managers understand when tests may be required, how testing is arranged, whom to contact, and how information is handled. Ensure the policy is reviewed for the jurisdictions and regulations that apply to your organization.

Select an operational process

A repeatable program should answer:

  • Who may authorize an order and how is it approved?
  • Which tests, specimen types, and collection methods are available?
  • How will random selections or other scheduled events be managed?
  • Who handles after-hours or post-accident coordination?
  • Who receives results and how is access restricted?

Prepare for exceptions

Think through what happens if a collection site is unavailable, an employee cannot attend, a form is incomplete, or a result requires review. Clarify escalation contacts before problems arise.

Review and improve

Revisit the program when regulations, operations, workforce roles, or vendor services change. Maintain appropriate records and privacy protections, and obtain qualified advice on compliance questions.

Related resources: Workplace testing · Policy support
